newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: INTERVIEW-Argentina's Fernandez touts growth, jobs.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Argentina's Fernandez touts growth, jobs.

text.p: Economy Minister Roque Fernandez said Argentina's economic recovery has been more robust than expected and vowed the government will now move quickly to create jobs and overcome the nation's "bad mood".

The minister, in an interview with Reuters, projected strong economic growth and falling unemployment during an election year, while disclosing that "conditions were right" to buy back foreign debt to lower Argentina's servicing costs.
"The economy is recovering strongly, more than we expected," Fernandez said. "We calculate the economy will grow by at least five percent in the second quarter."
That is smaller than the 8.1 percent year-on-year growth in the first quarter, but the economy early in the year rebounded from a weak base in January through March of 1996.
Growth for the year was earlier revised upward to six percent from five, but Fernandez said that may be exceeded.
"We always try to give conservative numbers because we don't want to give false expectations," he said. The annual rate "could be more than six percent."
The minister added that jobless data to be released July 18 should show a drop of one percentage point, to about 16.3 percent, from the last survey conducted in October.

"With 80 percent of the jobs poll finished, we have a fall of 1.5 points in the greater Buenos Aires area, which is the most populous in the country, and we think it will give us a fall of about one point for the whole country.

"That is within what we predicted, which was a fall of two points for the year," he added. "I don't know yet how much is due to job creation and how much to the change in the number of people looking for work. Still, I think that job creation will be a record."
On the weekend, Fernandez's chief aide Carlos Rodriguez said in a newspaper interview that a one percentage point drop in unemployment would imply that 100,000 jobs were created.

The Peronist government desperately needs good news on the 17.3 percent unemployment rate ahead of October's mid-term elections in Congress. The government has been hit by scores of demonstrations over unemployment in recent months.
Officials are considering several job creation projects. Congress has passed a bill to sell state mortgage bank Banco Hipotecario and use the estimated $3 billion in proceeds to finance public works.
It is studying a proposal to use $25 billion in public and private sector funds for construction projects and also a proposed $0.10 a liter hike in gasoline tax to build highways.

"There is concern about attacking social issues," he said. "It is an issue that we can't delay on. The bad mood (we have faced) in criticisms of the economic model is because we did not move quickly with that."
Fernandez said he expects the government, big business and labor to reach an agreement on labor reforms, designed to reduce unemployment, that can become law before October polls.
The government, the Group of Eight business chambers and the CGT main labor federation were set to meet late Monday to define where they agree and disagree on proposed reforms.

"I think it will be law before October and that the positions of the CGT and the G8 are not that different," Fernandez said. "When we go to the small print of the agreement, to the details, the positions will narrow."

The International Monetary Fund recommended labor reforms as a way of reducing employment costs, and President Carlos Menem tried to push a tough reform package through by decree. Blocked by courts and hostile unions, he tried three-way talks and when they proved fruitless, he made a deal with unions.
Late last month Menem went behind the backs of business leaders to sign a blueprint Act of Agreement with unions, a watered-down reform package.

The big business lobby blasted it as "useless" because it maintains union control over wage talks and drops plans to replace costly redundancy payouts with unemployment insurance. It also drops plans to force union-controlled health care plans to compete with private firms in an open market.
The ministry is also studying the possibility of buying back shorter-term debt that is of less interest to the market and for which investors demand higher interest payments.

"It is possible this year. The conditions are right. We cannot rule out that possibility," Fernandez said. "While the decision is not taken, there is a series of analyses that urge us to think about it seriously."
Brazil launched a buyback earlier this year in which investors were allowed to tender their par, discount or C bonds for a 30-year global bond issue.
